Un día pierde un estuche en el que guardaba su cartera, la cartilla bancaria y otros enseres personales e importantes para ella. Cuando recibe la llamada de una persona que alega tener su estuche, la señora Yeom corre directa a la estación de Seúl para recuperarla, donde se va a encontrar con que Dokgo, un indigente, es quien se la ha encontrado.
Para devolverle el favor y agradecerle las molestias, la ex profesora le dice al hombre que, cada vez que tenga hambre, no dude en pasarse por la tienda dado que siempre tendrán comida caliente para él. Por una serie de acontecimientos, Dokgo acabará trabajando en el turno nocturno para la señora Yeom.

Dokgo va a ir solucionando inconscientemente los problemas de la gente que frecuenta la tienda y esto, a su vez, va a provocar que el hombre recuerde su pasado y la historia que no recordaba que había dejado atrás.

Es una novela cortita que engancha y se lee muy rapidito. Me ha tenido bastante intrigada ya que me ha gustado bastante cómo está escrita, pero si que es verdad que creo que no he terminado de conectar con la historia ya que el plot twist final de la misma me ha resultado un poco raro.

Questo libro è al tempo stesso una coccola e un modo per aprire bene gli occhi sulla società in cui viviamo. Questo è reso possibile dal fatto che, attraverso le vicende dei vari personaggi, l'autore mette in luce molti problemi attuali ma allo stesso tempo lascia il lettore con una forte sensazione di speranza di miglioramento.

La trama volge tutta attorno a due elementi: Dokko, il protagonista, e il minimarket che da il titolo all'opera. Dokko è una persona alla quale probabilmente nessuno di noi rivolgerebbe più di uno sguardo, anzi ne saremmo anche impauriti: un senzatetto dall'aspetto imponente e minaccioso, con problemi nel parlare e nel ricordare per via di come lo ha ridotto la sua dipendenza da alcool. Eppure la signora Yeom lo premia per il suo buon cuore e lo aiuta a rialzarsi. Col tempo, Dokko si ripulisce, torna ad interagire con le persone, si appassiona al proprio lavoro più di chiunque altro. Torna alla vita. E a ricordare il proprio passato e la propria identità.

Ogni capitolo si concentra sulla storia di qualcuno legato al minimarket: clienti, impiegati, parenti degli impiegati, passanti; ognuno ha i propri pensieri e problemi e Dokko, con pochissimi gesti e parole, riesce a portare conforto e suggerimenti utili a risolverli. È un uomo strano, sicuramente, ma pian piano le persone vi si affezionano e si sentono grate nei suoi confronti.

Insomma, il libro evidenzia i pregiudizi e ci mette davanti alle seconde possibilità. Si parla di tante problematiche scottanti, e di una rinascita e crescita morale ed etica. Sul finale, ci si trova anche proiettati nella Storia Contemporanea, perché c'è uno stralcio del periodo Covid-19. Non sappiamo di preciso cosa accade alla fine a Dokko, ma il finale in qualche modo ci scalda il cuore perché lui ricorda e riconosce i propri sbagli passati e vuole ripartire da quelli per riscattarsi.

Fra gli argomenti toccati: la depressione, la pressione delle aspettative della società, l'alcolismo, le relazioni disfunzionali, la povertà, i pregiudizi, la violenza, la perdita di scopo ed ispirazione, la corruzione, la malasanità.

I was really intrigued when I read the synopsis of this. It’s unique and interesting, but it is very straightforward and to the point. At the core it really is about second chances and the characters reveal their internal struggles and work to overcome them.

Mrs. Yeom runs a convenience store and is kind to a homeless man who protected her lost wallet. She feeds him and gives him a job, much to the chagrin of her other employees. But he turns out to be so much more. He listens and is caring in turn, helping not only the other employees but customers that come to the store.

I loved the focus on second chances and people not being what they seem. Especially now, stories like this are important. It’s that reminder that we don’t know what other people are going through and to give them grace when we can. The characters in this book are flawed and have done things they’re not proud of, but speaking with this man helps them through it.

It just feels like there’s something missing. The book is very short, and while that’s not necessarily a bad thing, there are things that felt that a bit unresolved. The ending itself feels a little abrupt, and while it does give some insight into the homeless man it feels rushed. I think this could have really benefited from a little bit more character development and details.

The Second Chance Convenience Store is a warm, heartfelt novel that shines a light on the quiet power of kindness and community. Kim Ho-yeon crafts a story that feels both simple and profound, following Dok-go, a man with a troubled past, as he slowly finds a new sense of purpose working in Mrs. Yeom’s little neighborhood store. The relationship between these two characters is tender and moving, and the way the store becomes a safe haven for the community gives the book its charm.

What stands out most is the novel’s message: that even small acts of generosity can spark real transformation. The story is filled with moments of compassion, humor, and wisdom, and it leaves you with a sense of hope that lingers after the final page.

That said, the pacing can feel uneven at times, with stretches that move slowly, and some of the side characters could have been explored more deeply. The mystery surrounding Dok-go’s past also unfolds a little more predictably than expected.

Still, these are minor quibbles in what is otherwise a touching, uplifting book. Fans of cozy, character-driven fiction will find The Second Chance Convenience Store both comforting and inspiring—a reminder that second chances are possible, and that community can be life-changing.

Ao longo da narrativa nos deparamos com muitos conflitos pessoais e familiares e a contextualização da história durante a pandemia deram um ar de realidade satisfatório. A conexão com os personagens, porém, foi uma questão um tanto complicada, com exceção da senhora Yeom e o próprio Dok-go, os outros personagens tiveram uma evolução bem menos envolvente na trama.

O final narrado do ponto de vista do Dok-go foi bastante emocionante, o ponto alto da história, mas senti um pouco de falta de um desenvolvimento maior nessa parte, até para responder algumas questões que surgem inevitavelmente durante o desfecho, senti falta também do "final feliz" concretizado do Dok-go, ele merecia depois de todas as mudanças positivas que ele promoveu na vida das outras pessoas, mesmo quando ele próprio estava destruído e sem esperanças.

Realmente senti falta de alguns desfechos que seriam importantes, já que foram situações que se desenrolaram ao longo de toda a história.

Numa certa altura do livro senti a história um pouco arrastada, mas nada que prejudicasse o final que foi profundamente emocionante.

'The Second Chance Convenience Store' is a work that follows the tried and tested formula found in a lot of the cozy fiction in translation stories that are popular at the minute. The protagonist is facing hardship but with the help of a kind stranger they turn their life around whilst also unwittingly helping to turn the lives around of those they interact with. Each chapter is told from a different POV that tell a complete, interwoven story by the end. The fact the book follows this archetype is by no means a bad thing as I'm a massive fan of this type of story telling and enjoyed reading this.

I've found Korean 'healing fiction' can often be quite heavy handed with the self care and life advice it offers but I did find this story to be more subtle than most- well, except for the very last page where the lessons you're supposed to have learnt throughout the book and very explicitly stated just in case you missed them. More off-putting for me though, was how much of the final few pages of the story focus on COVID. Although the book was written around the time of the pandemic, it feels shoe horned in and really took me out of the story. I think ending the book on page 192 would have made for a much stronger ending- all of the plot threads are neatly tied together at this point and it would end as a real full circle moment.

Despite the ending being a bit jarring, I did enjoy this book and would recommend it for fans of cosy fiction who want an easy, heart warming read but something that's a little different to the other healing fiction stories out there.

Cálida y emocionante, La asombrosa tienda de la señora Yeom es una lectura que nos llena de esperanza. Ha sido la novela más vendida en Corea con más de un millón de ejemplares y se ha convertido en un auténtico éxito internacional.
El libro cuenta la historia de Dokgo, un hombre sin hogar que sufre de demencia debido a su adicción al alcohol. Dokgo tiene una "segunda oportunidad" cuando salva la billetera de la señora Yeom, dueña de una tienda de 24h. Dokgo también consigue un trabajo en el turno de noche en la tienda , lo que lo reúne con muchas personas, no solo con Yeom, sino también trabajadores y clientes. Este encuentro también le hizo recordar poco a poco su pasado. La mitad del libro está contada desde el punto de vista de varios personajes con sus propios problemas vitales. No fue hasta el último capítulo, cuando la historia fue escrita desde el propio punto de vista de Dokgo, y sabremos mucho más de él.
Me ha gustado mucho por todos los cambios por los que pasó Dokgo. También tenía heridas, heridas graves, hasta que finalmente pudo y estuvo dispuesto a aceptar y cambiar sus propios puntos de vista ante las personas que lo rodeaban. Si puede ayudar a otros a encontrar una salida siendo un buen oyente, entonces también debe ser capaz de encontrar soluciones a sus propios problemas.
En conclusión, un libro conmovedor lleno de emociones y que sin duda te enseñará a apreciar a los que tienes alrededor.

Ik vond het een fijn boek om te lezen, het is makkelijk leesbaar en heeft een duidelijke verhaallijn die goed te volgen is. Elk hoofdstuk gaat over iemand anders, dit vond ik erg leuk. Wel vond ik het jammer dat de hoofdstukken vaak open eindigde, wat mij betreft hadden ze nog wat langer mogen zijn en iets meer diepgang mogen hebben.
Het laatste hoofdstuk gaat over Dokgo zelf, ik vond het leuk om er eindelijk achter te komen hoe hij dakloos was geworden en wie hij daarvoor was. Wat ik jammer vond is dat dit voor mijn gevoel afgeraffeld was, het ging ineens heel snel. Ook werd voor mijn gevoel in dit hoofdstuk geprobeerd alles aan elkaar te koppelen van alle hoofdstukken waardoor de diepgang verloren ging, dit vond ik jammer.

Al met al is het een leuk verhaal en echt een feelgood zoals de kaft ook zegt, alleen mist er soms nog wat diepgang voor mijn gevoel.

All'inizio pensavo che si trattasse di un libro senza senso, uno di quelli che parlano della vita quotidiana senza una morale precisa. Anche quando ho iniziato a leggerlo mi è sembrato così, e mi stavo anche un po' annoiando, perché ci sono tanti nomi coreani illeggibili e molto simili tra loro.
Però, verso la metà del libro, ha iniziato a piacermi, perché non è proprio così ovvio come mi sembrava all'inizio. Il protagonista capisce di aver sbagliato in passato e, dopo aver vissuto per un lungo periodo come senzatetto, decide di migliorarsi.
Mi chiedevo – e me lo chiedo anche adesso – se si possa perdonare una persona che in passato ti ha fatto del male, ma che adesso lo ammette e decide di cambiare.
Mi pare che, scrivendo questa mia recensione, io abbia trovato la risposta al mio dubbio: perdonare sì, ma ricostruire il legame di prima no, però ovviamente dipende tutto dalla situazione.
Sinceramente rileggendo questa recensione per me non ha più senso, perché è tutto scollegato e non esprime pienamente quello che volevo scrivere, però la lascio così.

This book is an unexpected gem, verging on the saccharine but grounded in human foibles.

An older woman is on the train from Seoul to Busan, but realizes she has lost her purse. Just as she’s starting to panic, she gets a call from someone who has found it at Seoul Station. She turns around to go fetch it.

This is how Seongsu meets the homeless man Dokgo, and ends up offering him a job at the convenience store that she owns. His good deed in returning the purse has a cascading effect of good will that impacts the lives of workers, neighbors, and the families of these two.

The idea of the local convenience store as the source of major nutrition for a segment of society is very East Asian. The convenience store also serves as a nexus of connection.

This small book addresses a number of timely issues: family expectations, job security, alcoholism, plastic surgery, unconditional friendship.

So even if it’s kinda sweet, the story is also a guide for how one could things turn around when life isn’t going as hoped.
Because as is quoted in the book, via Bob Dylan’s grandmother, “Be kind, because everyone you’ll ever meet is fighting a hard battle.”

This was just the book I needed after some heavier ones left me in a bit of a reading slump!

This was a lovely “slice of life” book filled with compassion and empathy and a character - Dokgo (meaning lonely or single) - that I can only describe as Nanny McPhee-esque character ie “when you need him but do not want him he will stay, when you want him but no longer need him, he must go.”

Although I love this genre of book, I was pleased that Dokgo had some substance and wasn’t simply two dimensional. Some characters that full Dokgo’s role in other books I have enjoyed are supernatural or merely objects but that we have a living, breathing force for good in this novel is really refreshing.

There are so many elements of this book that are so relevant to our time and each character is in a predicament that we can relate to even if on the smallest scale.

As usual, any book with multiple perspectives that cross over - I very much enjoyed this! I was really excited to see that there is a sequel to this novel coming out and I will definitely be reading it when it’s published!

I gesti gentili si moltiplicano e scatenano una cascata di conseguenze positive per coloro che frequentano il piccolo esercizio commerciale.
Un romanzo che scalda il cuore. I personaggi riescono a superare il senso di abbandono, la solitudine, la rabbia e il rancore accettando la mano amica che viene loro porta disinteressatamente.

"D'altronde lei sapeva bene che un minimarket è un luogo dove le persone vanno e vengono. Dove tutti, che siano dipendenti o clienti, senza eccezioni, si fermano solo temporaneamente, dove potersi ricaricare, attraverso uno stipendio o i prodotti in vendita, come una stazione di servizio per le persone. In quella stazione di servizio, non solo avevo fatto il pieno, ma avevo anche riparato la mia auto. Una volta riparata, bisognava ripartire. Era tempo di tornare sulla strada. Een hartverwarmend verhaal over aandacht hebben en er zijn voor elkaar, niet alleen voor goede vrienden en familie, maar voor iedereen die op je pad komt. Als je op zoek bent naar een boek dat je gelukkig maakt en misschien zelfs nieuwe inzichten biedt, dan is dit zeker een aanrader. Ik lees vaak Japanse romans en literatuur, maar dit boek was mijn eerste kennismaking met een Koreaanse auteur. De schrijfstijl is minder dromerig en juist ‘recht voor z'n raap’, wat het soms grappig en lekker rauw maakte, maar ook toegankelijker. Het las onwijs prettig weg, zelfs als ik moe was. Dit smaakt dus zeker naar meer voor mij. De hoofdstukken hebben telkens een ander perspectief, wat ervoor zorgt dat het lekker wegleest en dat je verschillende emoties ervaart. Al met al heb ik enorm genoten van dit boek en ben ik blij dat ik het van de uitgever mocht ontvangen. Volgende maand komt er een nieuwe 'healing fiction' uit: 'Het restaurant van de herinneringen'. Ik ben ontzettend benieuwd!

Dokgo is dakloos, maar heeft het hart op de juiste plaats. Wanneer hij mevrouw Yeom (de eigenaresse van een plaatselijke buurtwinkel in Seoel) herenigt met haar gestolen tas, wil ze hem bedanken. Ze neemt hem mee naar haar winkel en vertelt hem dat er elke dag een maaltijd voor hem zal klaarstaan. Wanneer de man die de nachtdienst in de winkel op zich neemt ontslag neemt, mag Dokgo deze overnemen. Dokgo stottert en is zijn geheugen kwijt, dus in eerste instantie vinden collega’s en klanten hem wat raar. Maar onderschat nooit de kracht van onverwachte ontmoetingen…

Dit nieuwe genre heet healing fiction (of is het een nieuwe naam voor een bestaand genre?), en wat een treffende benaming! Dit boek is echt hartverwarmend en herstelt je geloof in de mensheid. Het verhaal laat zien wat er kan gebeuren wanneer je openstaat voor toevallige ontmoetingen en openhartige gesprekken met vreemden. Hoe je leven mooier kan worden wanneer je je niet laat leiden door vooroordelen.

Na de inleiding waarin we lezen hoe Dokgo en mevrouw Yeom elkaar leren kennen, wordt elk volgend hoofdstuk vanuit het perspectief van een ander personage verteld (denk hierbij aan mevrouw Yeom zelf, maar ook collega’s, klanten en familieleden passeren de revue). Dat zorgt ervoor dat het soms even schakelen is, maar de vlotte schrijfstijl loodst je hier zo doorheen. Elk personage heeft zijn/haar bagage en iets waarmee hij/zij worstelt (gevoelens, familierelaties, toekomstbeelden of gewoon zichzelf en het leven in het algemeen). Door een vriendelijk woord, een gevatte opmerking of een lief gebaar op het juiste moment kan je de moed vinden om verandering toe te staan. Ook het verhaal van Dokgo komt naarmate hij meer en meer zijn geheugen terugkrijgt aan bod, waar ik persoonlijk zelfs nog meer over had willen lezen en een beetje op mijn honger bleef zitten. Een puntje van kritiek dat dus eigenlijk ook een compliment is: het verhaal had gerust langer mogen zijn!

Mrs. Yeom is a seventy-year-old retired history teacher who lost her bag and it's returned to her by a homeless man with no memories of his past. Owner of a convenience store, she eventually hires him.

With fluid prose, Ho-yeon examines second chance and second family through a cast of characters whose lives intersect in an almost fateful way. At its core, this book is about kindness and community embodied through broken and struggling people trying to mend relationships. I am not sure if the story is supposed to have a redemptive arc as I was expecting a slightly different plot direction.

How can an act of kindness change someone?

With a melancholic touch, THE SECOND CHANCE CONVENIENCE STORE (tr. Janet Hong) reminds one to cling to the people/relationships one cherishes.

This book follows to beautiful tradition of being a slice of life with a poignant message. If you need a book to wrap you up in a warm hug and tell you that it will all be okay, then this is for you. The story follows several people from a conscience store that all get a second chance and, in turn, give second chances to others. It reminds us that everyone is going through their own battles and it is important to truly talk to the ones we love. Giving someone a second chance can change their life and it might even change yours. I love how the characters all helped each other (sometimes in a small way and sometimes in a big way). Each character is so fascinating to read and I love how complex they all are. None of them are truly angles and some of them have done some pretty bad stuff, but they are not devils either. The book points out that we can all make a change and help those around us.

A pesar de que es una historia corta, es de esas novelas que te dejan el corazón calentito. No esperaba que me fuera a gustar tanto.
Ha sido muy bonito leer cómo los personajes acababan encontrando una solución a sus problemas a través de la ayuda, al mismo tiempo que encuentran su propósito.
El hombre que deja de beber y mejora su situación en casa, la compañera de trabajo que encuentra otro trabajo que la ayuda a crecer, la otra compañera de trabajo que consigue mejorar la relación con su hijo. La actriz y escritora que consigue escribir la obra de su vida. Dokgo que, gracias a la ayuda de la señora Yeom, acaba descubriendo de nuevo quién es y consigue aprender de sus errores y luchar por arreglar las cosas.
Me ha parecido un detallazo enlazar esta historia con la pandemia, tiene muchísimo sentido con la historia de Dokgo y, además, le da realidad a la historia, como si hubiera pasado realmente.
La señora Yeom me ha parecido una mujer entrañable y fuerte que sabe lo que hace.
Es una lectura que te permite relajarte al mismo tiempo que te reconforta.

És senzillet i no té una qualitat literària espaterrant, però no està gens malament. És d’aquells llibres que llegir-los et fa sentir bé, com una llar de foc encesa o un coixí tovet i net on arrepenjar-hi el cap mentre a fora plou.

El protagonista és un home sense sostre que, després d’una bona obra, és recompensat amb escreix per una dona que li ofereix feina. A partir d’aquí, l’home demostra tenir un cor noble i les seves paraules i gestos ajuden i milloren la vida de molts del seu voltant. I això permet que la seva memòria, bloquejada per l’alcohol i l’angoixa, com un roc de gel, vagi desfent-se amb aquest escalf humà. I, així, recupera la seva identitat, amb tot de llums i ombres, de manera que pot enfrontar-les i sortir-ne millor persona.

Potser el missatge és massa simple i pronosticable (la força de l’amor i del bé, i com un petit gest pot desencadenar tot de bones accions amb repercussió positiva per a tothom), però no per això deixa de ser bonic. Un llibre “feelgood” de manual.

Mrs Yeom loses a bag containing her wallet at Seoul station and returns to discover that Dokgo, who found it for her, is homeless and has no recollection of who he was before he came to Seoul. She hires Dokgo to cover the night shift at her convenience store - and never once does she regret it. Giving Dokgo a second chance will cause a ripple effect of second chances for others.

This book will make you believe that kindness can change the world - even if it starts as a simple, small act. I certainly believe. Dokgo was such a fascinating, mysterious character. I was almost disappointed to find out about his past towards the end, though it was handled so well. I have a keen interest in COVID-19 fiction and this certainly fits the bill, but I also admired the message about taking our kindness with us into such an uncertain global situation.

A beautiful reminder that a little kindness goes a long way

The Second Chance Convenience Store by Kim Ho-yeon is a soul soothing addition to the "healing fiction" genre that has been taking the literary world by storm. It’s the literary equivalent of a warm bowl of soup on a rainy afternoon simple, comforting, and surprisingly nourishing.

It’s cozy, nostalgic, and makes you want to go buy a bottle of corn silk tea immediately.
It doesn’t rely on grand gestures; instead, it shows how simple, authentic human connection can fix the cracks in our lives.

It’s a bit sentimental and the pacing is gentle, so don’t expect a high-octane plot. But if you’re looking for a "hug in a book" to help you decompress, this is it.
A solid 4 stars for anyone needing a reminder that second chances are possible.

Having enjoyed Before the Coffee Gets Cold, I thought I’d enjoy this too, as it looked like a similar laid back story and theme with rich characters… but unfortunately I didn’t enjoy this book at all.

I found the pacing to be far too slow. The characters were pretty simple, but their descriptions and interactions felt so drawn out and laborious to read. The premise was hard to accept too; a homeless guy who meanders around with a fairly blasé attitude that somehow transforms the lives of people he briefly interacts with… it all felt a bit far-fetched. As for the ending, I guess it kind of made some sense, but it was a bit random, and it would’ve been nicer to have some of the answers distributed through the book rather than just all at the end.

I very nearly DNFd this book several times, and skim read parts of it just to see if it was worth carrying on with. But overall I just found it to be really boring. It’s not a bad book per se, but it’s definitely not for me.
